title: The Questions That Actually Separate Japanese Language Schools
summary: Location, price and photos are the easy comparison and the least useful one. Four things separate schools in ways you will feel every day for two years.
body_html:
Comparison tables line schools up on location, tuition and intake months. Those are the facts that are easy to tabulate, not the facts that decide how your two years go.

Here are four axes that do, each read off what schools actually publish.

1. Capacity, read as parallel classes

Capacity looks like a vanity number. It is really a proxy for something you will feel every week: how many classes run at your level.

The spread among schools is wider than people expect. Human Academy's Tokyo campus states a capacity of 2,440. [source:1] In one group of three schools, the preparation course states a capacity of 1,728, the graduate-school course a capacity of 900, and the employment course a capacity of 100. [source:2] [source:3] [source:4]

A school built for 100 students runs a handful of classes. [source:4] One built for 2,440 runs dozens. [source:1] If your Japanese sits between two levels, the large school probably has a third option and the small one does not.

What you give up at scale is everything outside the classroom: university advice, visa paperwork questions, the conversation where your situation turns out to be unusual. So the question to ask is not "how big are you" but how many students does one advisor handle. A large school that answers that clearly is a different proposition from one that does not.

2. What the course is for, not what it teaches

Every school teaches Japanese. The useful distinction is what the course is pointed at, and some schools make this structural.

In the Sendagaya group, the three schools run different tracks: a university-preparation course, a graduate-school course, and an employment course. [source:2] [source:3] [source:4] They are not branches of one school with the same curriculum.

The content follows. The preparation course covers EJU and JLPT preparation and the basic subjects those exams test in Japanese, plus the statement of purpose and the interview. [source:2] The graduate-school course teaches writing logically for the entrance essay, for post-admission reports and for a master's thesis, with repeated practice at writing to a set length under time pressure. [source:3]

If you enrol in the wrong one, you are not getting worse teaching. You are paying for exam preparation or thesis writing you do not need, and not getting the thing you do.

So: name your destination before you shortlist. Then ask each school which of its courses is for that destination — and if the answer is "all of them", you have learned something.

3. Divided by campus, or divided by programme

This one is invisible until it matters, and schools sit on opposite sides of it.

ISI separates purposes across campuses. Its Tokyo campuses include an academic campus and career campuses, with the purpose in the campus name, and it also operates outside Tokyo. [source:5]

Akamonkai separates purposes inside one school: a general study-abroad course, a preparatory education course, a business employment class, employment support, and a named corporate ICT programme. [source:6]

Both are reasonable. They differ in what happens when your plan changes — and plans change often, usually around the six-month mark when people discover what they actually want.

Under the campus model, changing track can mean changing campus, which means changing commute and classmates. Under the programme model, it means changing class. Ask the question before you need the answer: if my goal changes after six months, what actually happens?

4. Accommodation: owned, or introduced

"Accommodation support" covers two different relationships, and a tick in a comparison table hides which one you get.

Akamonkai states that it owns and manages a large number of student dormitories, with rent from 40,000 to 60,000 yen per month and utilities charged separately on usage. [source:6] Kyoshin Language Academy's housing page is for share house and homestay introduction. [source:7]

Owning and introducing are not the same. One gives you a landlord who is also your school; the other gives you a third-party contract on the operator's terms.

And even within the owned model, read the allocation rule. Akamonkai asks which dormitory you would like and states plainly that you may be assigned a different one. [source:6] The Sendagaya group sets out its sequence: you give first, second and third choices, and about 2 months before enrolment you are told which could be reserved, with a cancellation fee after that. [source:8]

So the honest framing is that a dormitory is allocated, not chosen — and you commit before you have seen it.

The eligibility question that outranks all four

None of the above matters if the school cannot take you, and two things can make that so.

If your prior schooling runs fewer than 12 years, you need a course with the Ministry of Education's preparatory designation — a short list that specific schools hold. [source:2]

And separately, every school is operating under one of two systems right now, one of which is being abolished. That is a question to settle before any comparison, and it is covered in is your school legally allowed to take you.

What to ask, in one email

  • How many parallel classes run at my level in the intake I am applying for?
  • How many students does one advisor handle?
  • Which of your courses is for my destination, and what does it cover that the others do not?
  • If my goal changes after six months, what happens — new class, new campus, or wait for the next intake?
  • Do you own the accommodation or introduce it? What is included, and can I decline after allocation?
  • Are you accredited under the new system, or notified during the transition?
  • What is the current fee schedule for my intake, in writing?

A school that answers these in one reply has told you more than any brochure. One that answers three of seven has also told you something.

For how to read what a school's own site does and does not say, see what a school not publishing something tells you. The two schools above are compared directly in Akamonkai and ISI, and the three-track group in the Sendagaya comparison. Dormitory specifics: the schools that provide them.

Everything above comes from the schools' own pages, linked below, and changes by academic year. We prepare and forward application documents — admission is decided by the school, and tuition is paid directly to it.

claims_without_sources: 「定員が並行クラス数の代理指標になる」という読み方 —— 学校は並行クラス数を公表しておらず、定員からの推論である。本文でも「probably」と書き、断定していない。学校に直接聞けという形にしてある。
「規模が大きいほど教室外の対応が薄くなる」—— 一般的な帰結であり、学校の記述でも検証済みの相関でもない。だからこそ「一人の担当が何人見るか」を聞けという問いの形にした。
「計画はたいてい半年あたりで変わる」—— 当方の経験則であって出典がない。数字を伴う主張にしないよう「often」と書いた。
赤門会の企業名を冠した ICT プログラムの具体名 —— 学校は掲げているが、本サイトが特定企業との関係を保証しているような含意を避けるため企業名を出していない。
ISI の各校区の定員・学費 —— 本記事では触れていない。学費は別記事で出典付きに扱っている。
7 つの質問に答える学校のほうが良い学校である、という因果 —— 検証していない。「答えないこともまた情報である」という以上のことは言っていない。
